content:
A respected aviation directory has cut the number of Indian Air Force Rafale fighters it counts as active to 32, down from 35 in its previous edition and from the 36 aircraft India bought from France — a revision that has revived a politically charged argument about what happened to the fleet during last year's brief war with Pakistan.

The 2027 edition of FlightGlobal's World Air Forces directory, published this month and compiled using data from the aviation intelligence firm Cirium, lists 32 Rafales as active with the Indian Air Force, according to [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/iafs-active-rafale-count-cut-to-32-by-flightglobal-defence-ministry-disputes-claim/article71720440.ece). The previous edition, published in late 2025 after Operation Sindoor, had listed 35. India procured 36 Rafales in total — 28 single-seat EH variants and eight twin-seat DH aircraft — under a 2016 government-to-government deal with France.

India's Defence Ministry has pushed back. Senior officials told The Hindu that the figures published in the directory did not originate from the ministry or the Air Force, and questioned the authenticity of the assessment. The directory itself offers no explanation for the change: it does not say which aircraft were removed from the active column, or why.

That silence matters, because the number sits at the centre of an unresolved dispute. During the four-day aerial clash between India and Pakistan in May 2025, Pakistan claimed to have shot down several Indian aircraft, including Rafales. India has acknowledged only one visually corroborated Rafale loss, which the 2026 edition of the directory appeared to reflect when it reduced the count from 36 to 35. The latest cut to 32 implies three more aircraft are no longer counted as active — but neither FlightGlobal nor Cirium has said whether that reflects combat damage, aircraft in long-term maintenance, or simply a change in how the data was classified.

Former Air Force vice chief Air Marshal Narmdeshwar Tiwari, who was the service's deputy chief during Operation Sindoor, called the assessment "patently false" and said the publication should re-evaluate its sources, according to Scroll. The ministry's own evidence points the other way: in June this year the Air Force issued a tender seeking "bridge support" for all 36 Rafale aircraft, a contract that would make little sense if four of them were no longer in service.

The directory's revisions are not confined to India. The same edition also cut Pakistan's fleet of Saab 2000 Erieye airborne early-warning aircraft from nine to seven, again without explanation. The parallel changes invite comparison with the claims both sides made during the May 2025 confrontation, but, as Outlook India noted, neither revision establishes confirmed combat losses on either side.

The figures also sit uneasily alongside other independent counts. The Global Institute for National Capability's Defence Index lists all 36 Indian Rafales as active, and the same FlightGlobal edition lists 263 Su-30MKI fighters with the Indian Air Force — a figure higher than the 258 to 260 widely reported by other sources. That inconsistency is the point the directory's defenders make in its favour, and its critics make against it: these directories are estimation baselines built from open-source fleet tracking, diplomatic reporting, satellite imagery and the accumulation of unverified claims over a year, not official disclosures.

What "active" means is doing much of the work here. Fleet trackers like Cirium routinely apply conservative deductions when aircraft disappear from observable service for a period — for heavy maintenance, upgrades or accident repairs — even when no loss has occurred. A jet in a hangar for a scheduled overhaul and a jet destroyed in combat can look identical in a database for months. Until Cirium explains its airframe-level classifications, the number 32 is an estimate of what can be observed, not a count of what India has lost.

That distinction has not stopped the figure from becoming political. Operation Sindoor remains the most sensitive episode in Indian defence politics since the 2019 Balakot strikes, and the Rafale — bought in a deal that itself survived years of opposition attacks over price and process — is the most scrutinised aircraft in the Indian inventory. Every revision of the count is read in New Delhi as a verdict on the operation, and in Islamabad as a scorecard.

The episode also illustrates a wider problem with open-source military accounting. As the world's air forces grow more secretive about losses and more reliant on commercial data, the directories that journalists and analysts depend on are increasingly forced to choose between publishing a number they cannot fully explain and publishing nothing at all. FlightGlobal chose the former, and the argument that followed was, in a sense, the price of that choice.

For now, the official position is clear: India's Defence Ministry says all 36 Rafales remain in the fleet, and the directory's compilers have offered no evidence to the contrary. The burden of proof, in the absence of an explanation, rests with the number itself — and the number, for now, is silent on what it actually means. For more on how the region's air forces are changing, see our coverage of [Russia's violation of Polish airspace](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russia-violates-poland-airspace-missiles-drone-november-20-2026) and the [IMF's warning on global debt](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/imf-georgieva-global-debt-100-percent-gdp-november-2026).
summary: The latest edition of FlightGlobal's World Air Forces directory lists just 32 of India's 36 Rafale fighters as active, down from 35 a year ago, reviving questions about the fleet after the May 2025 clash with Pakistan — but India's Defence Ministry says the figures did not come from the Air Force, and neither the directory nor its data provider has explained the revision.
title: FlightGlobal cuts India's active Rafale fleet to 32 — but New Delhi disputes the count
